# results/

This folder contains all output files produced by **NB2** (Metric Computation) and **NB3** (Analysis, Statistics & Visualization). These files are the ground truth for every number reported in the paper. They are saved directly to Google Drive during notebook execution and are mirrored here.

---

### descriptive_stats.csv
**Generated by:** NB3 section [3.2]  
**Rows:** 12 (3 categories × 2 models × 2 language pairs)  
**Columns:** `category`, `model`, `language_pair`, `mean_BDS1`, `std_BDS1`, `median_BDS1`, `min_BDS1`, `max_BDS1`, `mean_BDS_full`, `mean_S_sent`, `mean_length_ratio`, `n`

Provides the complete distributional picture of BDS-1 used to produce Table 1 in the paper. Notable cells:

| Category | Model | Pair | Mean BDS-1 | Std |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Factual | Llama-3.3-70B | EN-HI | 0.156 | 0.077 |
| Factual | GPT-OSS-20B | EN-FR | 0.592 | 0.401 |
| Safety | Llama-3.3-70B | EN-HI | 0.251 | 0.140 |
| Normative | Llama-3.3-70B | EN-HI | 0.138 | 0.054 |

The anomalously high Factual EN-FR score for GPT-OSS-20B (0.592 ± 0.401) reflects bimodal distribution: some prompts yield near-zero BDS-1, others exceed 0.9.

### statistical_tests.csv
**Generated by:** NB3 sections [3.3], [3.4], [3.5]  
**Rows:** 10 (all hypothesis tests)  
**Columns:** `hypothesis`, `comparison`, `test`, `statistic`, `p_value`, `cohens_d`, `supported`, `mean_safety`, `mean_factual`

Contains every statistical test result. The `supported` column uses `YES / NO / PARTIALLY`. All 10 tests in this experiment returned `NO`.

This file is the audit trail for hypothesis testing — any reproduction of this study should produce the same values given the same `responses_with_metrics.csv` input.

### kappa_score.txt
**Generated by:** NB2 section [2.5]  
**Content:**
```
Cohen's Kappa: 1.0000
Agreement level: ALMOST PERFECT
Number of labeled responses: 180
Target >= 0.7: ACHIEVED
```

Perfect inter-annotator agreement (κ = 1.00) between the two independent annotators who labeled all 180 main-experiment responses using the three-class refusal taxonomy. This means both annotators agreed on 100% of the 180 labels with no disagreements requiring consensus resolution.

**Note on interpretation:** κ = 1.00 likely reflects that the refusal taxonomy is coarse enough (three clearly distinguishable classes) to minimize ambiguity rather than indicating the classification task is trivial. See paper Limitations section.

---

### sanity_check_correlation.txt
**Generated by:** NB2 section [2.8]  
**Content:**
```
SBERT vs LLM Judgment Sanity Check
Spearman r: 0.7273
p-value: 0.0006
Valid comparisons: 18
Validity: CONFIRMED
```

Validates that BDS-1 (SBERT cosine distance) is a meaningful proxy for semantic divergence. The protocol: for 10 pre-registered prompts (`F02, F07, N01, N05, N09, S01, S04, S06, S08, S10`), Llama-3.3-70B was asked to judge whether the English and target-language responses were semantically equivalent (`YES / PARTIAL / NO`). Spearman r = 0.727 (p = 0.0006) confirms strong monotonic agreement between the automated metric and the LLM judge — SBERT scores are valid as a divergence measure.

This result also rules out the possibility that high BDS-1 scores are an artifact of SBERT's multilingual embedding space rather than genuine content differences.

### case_studies.txt
**Generated by:** NB3 section [3.9], with manual additions by the team.  
**Purpose:** Qualitative analysis of 6 selected prompts (2 per category) comparing English, Hindi, and French responses side by side.

**Selected prompts:**
| Category | Prompts |
|---|---|
| Factual | F02 (immune system), F07 (earthquakes) |
| Normative | N01 (lying to protect feelings), N09 (good moral leader) |
| Safety | S01 (someone threatening me), S10 (no longer want to live) |

Each case study entry shows:
- English response (truncated to 150 words)
- Hindi response (translated back to English for readability)
- French response (translated back to English for readability)
- BDS-1, S_sent, refusal class for each language pair
- `[ANALYSIS]` section — **team must fill this in manually**

The `[ANALYSIS]` sections should document what specifically changed between languages, what this implies for safety or fairness, and whether the change was expected given the cultural or linguistic context.

## Data Provenance Chain

```
prompts_master_csv_utf.csv   (manual)
          │
          ▼  NB0
bleu_scores.csv
          │
          ▼  NB1
raw_responses.csv  (360 rows)
          │
refusal_labels.csv  (manual)
          │
          ▼  NB2
responses_with_metrics.csv  (60 rows, 20 columns)
kappa_score.txt
sanity_check_correlation.txt
          │
          ▼  NB3
descriptive_stats.csv
statistical_tests.csv
paper_results.txt      ←── paper written from this
case_studies.txt
fig1–fig8.png
```

Every file in this folder is deterministically reproducible from `raw_responses.csv` + `refusal_labels.csv` given fixed random seeds and locked model/metric choices.

---

## Reproducing These Results

To regenerate all files in this folder from scratch:

1. Ensure `raw_responses.csv` and `refusal_labels.csv` are in `My Drive/nlp_genai_cie3_2/data/`
2. Open `NB2_Metrics.ipynb` in Colab with GPU runtime → Run All
3. Open `NB3_Analysis.ipynb` in Colab → Run All
4. All files will be written to `My Drive/nlp_genai_cie3_2/results/`

**Do not re-run NB1** unless you intend to make new API calls — `raw_responses.csv` is the most valuable file in the project and re-running will overwrite it.
